name: KeyDB

status.note: Last release 6.3.4 in October 2023 and last commit to main in April 2024; keydb.dev now only points to the docs repository on GitHub.

summary: A multithreaded fork of Redis, owned by Snap, that serves one dataset from several threads and adds active-active replication and an experimental flash tier.
intro: KeyDB began in 2019 as a fork of Redis by developers who wanted it to use more than one CPU core. It runs the normal Redis event loop on several threads (`server-threads`); each client connection is pinned to a thread when it is accepted, and access to the shared hash table is guarded by a spinlock, held for the length of `EXEC` in a transaction. It speaks the Redis protocol and runs Redis modules and Lua scripts, so clients and tools work unchanged, and an MVCC design lets commands such as `KEYS` and `SCAN` run without blocking the rest of the database.

It adds features Redis doesn’t have. With `active-replica yes`, a replica also accepts writes, and two servers can be replicas of each other; every write is timestamped and, after a broken link heals, the newest write wins. More than two masters must be fully meshed, or data is lost. KeyDB on FLASH, built on RocksDB and still labelled experimental, writes all data to SSD and keeps hot keys in RAM, so a dataset can outgrow memory.

Snap, which already ran KeyDB in its caching infrastructure, took it over in 2021 and in May 2022 released the formerly paid Pro and Enterprise features as one BSD-3-Clause project, version 6.3.0. There is no commercial edition or paid support. Activity has since slowed: 6.3.4 in October 2023 is the latest release, the main branch last changed in April 2024, and both keydb.dev and docs.keydb.dev now just redirect to the KeyDB-docs repository. Valkey is the actively maintained BSD-licensed Redis fork.
strengths: Several threads on one node, so one server can use more cores without sharding
A drop-in replacement for Redis: same protocol, modules and scripts
Active-active replication between two nodes, with the newest write winning after a split
BSD-3-Clause, with the former enterprise features included
limits: Little development since 2024: no release since October 2023 and no paid support
Its 6.3 releases track Redis 6-era behaviour, so commands and fixes added to Redis and Valkey since are missing
Active replication resolves conflicts by timestamp, so concurrent writes to the same key on two masters lose one of them
The flash tier is still marked experimental

specs.query-language: Redis commands, Lua scripts and modules
specs.replication: Redis replication, plus active-active replicas where the newest write wins
specs.storage-engine: In memory; experimental FLASH tier on RocksDB

snippet.title: keydb.conf for two servers that replicate to each other
source: # on server A (10.0.0.1); server B mirrors this with replicaof 10.0.0.1
active-replica yes          # this replica also accepts writes
replicaof 10.0.0.2 6379     # replicate from B, while B replicates from A
# optional: keep the dataset on SSD, hot keys in RAM (experimental)

story: Redis runs its commands on a single event loop, which keeps its code simple but leaves most of a big server’s cores idle. In 2019 its developers forked it as KeyDB with a different philosophy: Redis, they argued, kept the code simple “at the expense of complexity for the user”, who then had to run clusters and Sentinel to use more hardware. KeyDB took on the harder code so a single node could do more, and added active replication and a flash storage tier, some of them in paid Pro and Enterprise editions.

Snap used KeyDB in its caching infrastructure and took the project over in 2021. In May 2022 it open-sourced everything as one BSD-3-Clause project with release 6.3.0. Releases continued until 6.3.4 in October 2023; commits to the main branch stopped in April 2024, By then the Linux Foundation had forked Redis as Valkey, also BSD-licensed, after Redis changed its licence in 2024.

choices.choice: Run the Redis event loop on several threads
choices.why: Users wanted more throughput from one machine without sharding. Pinning each connection to a thread and guarding the shared hash table with a short spinlock kept most of Redis’s code and semantics.
With active replication a hot spare is already writable, so failover needs no promotion step; timestamps decide which write wins after a split.

choices.choice: Open-source the enterprise features at Snap
choices.why: Once Snap owned it, there was no paid product to protect, so the project merged both editions into one BSD-licensed codebase.

timeline.text: KeyDB forks Redis to add multithreading
Version 6.3.0 open-sources the former enterprise features under BSD-3-Clause
Release 6.3.4 in October, the latest so far
Last commit to the main branch, in April
